title: ergonomic-multi-tool-exec-surface-with-deterministic-injection-and-retry-policies
author: Maya Chen
release_notes: Adds ergonomic multi-tool execution API with deterministic tool result injection, per-tool retry policies, and OpenAI function-calling compatibility shim. No breaking changes; opt-in behind feature flag 'multi_tool_exec_v1'.
description:
Motivation: Customers building chains of tools and function calls requested a simpler, deterministic execution surface for multi-tool workflows that preserves streaming semantics and is compatible with OpenAI-style function calling. This PR introduces a developer-facing API for batching/parallelizing tool calls while guaranteeing deterministic result injection into model context, plus per-tool retry policies and a compatibility shim for existing OpenAI integrations.

What this PR does (single continuous description): Introduces a new request-level field 'tool_execution' (opt-in via query param or SDK flag) that supports two modes: 'sequential' (default behavior preserved) and 'parallel-safe' (parallel invocation with deterministic, stable injection order). The implementation provides: 1) deterministic injection: tool results are injected into the model context in a stable ordering derived from the original tool list and logical dependencies; 2) streaming passthrough for tool stdout/structured outputs: partial tool outputs stream back to the client while the model continues generation, with clear markers for tool boundaries; 3) per-tool retry policies: each tool entry can include a retry configuration (max_attempts, backoff_ms, retry_on) applied by the orchestrator; 4) idempotency tokens and result caching hooks so repeated requests do not re-execute costly side-effectful tools; 5) OpenAI compatibility mapping: 'tool_execution' maps to an enhanced 'function_call' shim for the compatibility layer, allowing existing OpenAI clients to opt into parallel-safe behavior without changing call-sites.

API surface changes and examples: The PR extends the Redwood JSON request envelope with optional top-level keys for tooling. Example (compact, single-line for docs): {"input":"Translate and summarize","tool_execution":{"mode":"parallel-safe","tools":[{"name":"translate","idempotency_key":"tx-123","retry":{"max_attempts":2,"backoff_ms":200},"stream":true},{"name":"summarize","retry":{"max_attempts":1}}],"inject_results":"deterministic"}}. SDK helpers are added for Python/TS to build the envelope. For OpenAI compatibility, a header 'X-Redwood-Tool-Exec: parallel-safe' enables shim behavior that accepts function_call payloads and converts them to 'tool_execution' internally.

Implementation notes: Runtime changes are contained to the request router, orchestrator, and streaming layer. The orchestrator now understands a logical DAG of tool dependencies (lightweight: ordered list + optional 'after' field) and executes independent tools concurrently up to a configurable concurrency limit (default 4). The streaming layer was updated to tag events with 'tool_start', 'tool_chunk', 'tool_end', and 'injection_point' events so clients can reliably rehydrate partial results and visualize mid-flight tool progress. To preserve deterministic injection we collect completed tool outputs into an ordered buffer and inject into the model context at the earliest allowed injection point (stream boundary or end of turn) according to the 'inject_results' policy.

Retries and side-effects: The orchestrator supports per-tool retry rules. For tools declared as side-effectful, an idempotency_key is required; if missing, the PR's validation layer rejects the request with a descriptive 422 error. Retryable errors are classified with a pluggable list (e.g., transient network, 5xx, timeouts). Exponential jitter/backoff is applied; retries are limited by a total request timeout to avoid unbounded execution.

Migration and backward compatibility: Default behavior remains unchanged. 'tool_execution' is opt-in. The OpenAI shim allows existing function_call users to flip a header to get enhanced behavior, but the shim makes conservative assumptions about ordering and will fall back to sequential mode when function metadata implies side effects or unknown idempotency.

Rollout plan: Feature gated behind 'multi_tool_exec_v1'. Stage 1 (internal dogfood): enable for 10% of host accounts and Redwood internal services (2 days). Stage 2 (beta): enable for opt-in customers and give SDK flag (2 weeks). Stage 3: wider rollout with metrics guardrails (latency, error rate) and opt-out available.

Testing and CI: Added unit tests for orchestrator scheduling, deterministic injection buffer, retry semantics, and streaming event tagging. Integration tests added to the eval-harness targeting both parallel-safe and sequential modes with synthetic tool stubs (fast, slow, failing). CI: all checks passing after one flake rerun (see CI summary).

Performance: End-to-end lab runs with bench harness show median end-to-end latency for a 3-tool parallel-safe job decreased 18% vs naive sequential execution, and p95 improved by 9% for independent-tool workloads. For highly dependent chains, overhead from buffering is ~6% median latency increase, which is documented and acceptable for deterministic ordering.

Security and auditing: Tool invocations include audit metadata (caller, request_id, tool_name) forwarded to the audit-log-exporter. Private deployments will need an updated policy to allow the streaming markers through firewalls; notes added to installer docs.

Open items and future work: - Automatic DAG extraction from model annotations - Adaptive concurrency tuning based on token budget - Better UX for partial result synthesis in Console (follow-up PR)

Commit summary: 6 commits: initial API schema and validation, orchestrator scheduling engine, streaming event tagging, OpenAI compatibility shim, SDK helpers + tests, docs and changelog.

ui_changes: Console: new visualization for streaming tool events with timeline and per-tool status. Docs: quickstart and migration guide added.

incident_tieins: This PR addresses fragility surfaced during INC-2026 where parallel tool invocations caused non-deterministic context injections during a high-traffic canary.
